summary: Discusses where constraint-based LDP (CR-LDP) is useful, which extensions to LDP it needs, and how to deploy it, along with known limitations. It was written to support advancing CR-LDP on the standards track. It is informational.

eli5.summary: This explains what a particular network tool is for, how to use it, and what it cannot do, so builders know if it fits.

subtitle: Where constraint-based LDP (CR-LDP) fits in MPLS traffic engineering, what it needs from LDP, and its limits.

tldr.problem: Standards-track advancement of CR-LDP required a statement of where the protocol is useful, what it requires, and what it cannot do.
tldr.mechanism: This applicability statement describes CR-LDP as extensions to LDP for setting up explicitly routed LSPs over TCP, lists the LDP modes it needs, and gives deployment guidance.
tldr.outcome: CR-LDP suits networks with very large numbers of LSPs. It supports only point-to-point, unidirectional setups with one label allocation per setup.

facts.label: Steady state per LSP
facts.value: As little as 200 bytes or less

facts.label: Required LDP mode combination
facts.value: Downstream On Demand Ordered with Conservative Label Retention

sections.title: What CR-LDP Is
sections.content:
CR-LDP is described as a simple, scalable, open, non-proprietary traffic engineering signaling protocol for MPLS IP networks. It establishes explicitly routed Label Switched Paths (LSPs) through extensions to LDP. Because LDP is peer-to-peer and built on TCP sessions, CR-LDP messages are reliably delivered and flow controlled, and state for explicitly routed LSPs does not need periodic refresh.

Optional capabilities cover bandwidth allocation and setup and holding priorities, and these can be changed without disrupting an in-service LSP. The signaled parameters, together with edge traffic conditioning functions, can describe QoS scenarios such as IP differentiated services, integrated services, ATM service classes and frame relay.

The statement does not prevent other signaling protocols. CR-LDP and RSVP-TE do similar jobs, no consensus exists on which is technically superior, and administrators should choose for their situation. The RSVP-TE side is covered in RFC 3210.
sections.eli5: CR-LDP builds reserved routes through a network using a reliable messaging channel, so it does not have to keep reminding everyone the route is still there.

sections.title: Where the Extensions Apply
sections.content:
CR-LDP extensions are defined so they translate directly to objects and messages in other protocols with similar services. Implementations can use this to set up LSPs for an aggregate service, to translate messages for a non-CR-LDP part of the network, and to describe a wide range of QoS services.

Steady state information for an LSP may be as little as 200 bytes or less, and implementations may support more than one hundred thousand or one million LSPs through a single label switching router (LSR) under stable conditions. The low per-LSP state and control traffic make CR-LDP applicable where very large numbers of LSPs are switched at each LSR, such as large backbones using MPLS to carry many traffic streams between a moderately large number of edge nodes. It may also mediate between networks that use different signaling models.
sections.eli5: Each route needs only a tiny note kept about it, so a router can remember a huge number of routes at once.

sections.title: Deployment and LDP Modes
sections.content:
LDP defines six label distribution and management modes: Downstream On Demand, Downstream Unsolicited, Independent Control, Ordered Control, Conservative Label Retention and Liberal Label Retention. In networks that only need traffic engineered LSPs, CR-LDP does not need all of LDP. The basic Discovery, Session and Notification messages are required, plus one specific combination: Downstream On Demand Ordered label distribution with Conservative Label Retention.

Downstream Unsolicited and Independent Control are not required for strict explicit routes. CR-LDP also supports loose explicit routes, which let an operator define a path through parts of a network without full topology knowledge. Used well, this can help CR-LDP interoperate with plain LDP. Implementations MAY support loose explicit routes using Abstract Nodes or Hierarchical Explicit Routing without LDP hop-by-hop setup.

Where both hop-by-hop and traffic engineered LSPs are needed, one protocol, LDP with the CR-LDP extensions, can serve both, so no new protocol has to be introduced for TE-LSP signaling.
sections.eli5: You do not need every feature of the base tool, just one specific way of working. If you also need ordinary routes, the same tool handles both.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: The CR-LDP specification supports only point-to-point LSPs. Multipoint-to-point and point-to-multipoint are for further study (FFS). It supports only unidirectional LSP setup, with bidirectional setup also FFS. It supports only a unique label allocation per LSP setup, and multiple label allocations per setup are FFS.
sections.eli5: For now it builds one-way roads between two points, one road at a time. Fancier shapes are left for later.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The memo introduces no additional security issues. As an extension to LDP, CR-LDP shares the security concerns associated with LDP.
sections.eli5: It is built on the base tool, so it worries about the same safety problems that tool does.
